Knoxville by the numbers

Who bills property tax on a Knoxville house?

Two governments send a bill, and the Knox County Property Assessor sets the value behind both. A house inside the city limits owes Knox County tax and City of Knoxville tax, each collected by a different office. Keep the two bills separate, because the city says plainly that payments sent to the wrong office cause errors.

  • City bill: the City of Knoxville Revenue Office, phone 865-215-2084, Suite 453 of the City County Building at 400 Main Street, open weekdays, 8:00 to 4:30. Mail goes to P.O. Box 15001, Knoxville, TN 37901-5001.
  • County bill: the Knox County Trustee, phone 865-215-2305, Suite 427 of the same building, with matching weekday hours. Mail goes to P.O. Box 70, Knoxville, TN 37901, and the Trustee runs six locations.
  • Value questions: the Knox County Property Assessor, 865-215-2360.
  • Deed questions: the Register of Deeds, 865-215-2330.

The city's property tax page lists these contacts side by side, and the county's Trustee page covers the county side.

What is Knoxville like, and how does it affect a sale?

Knoxville sits in the Tennessee Valley, roughly halfway between the Great Smoky Mountains and the Cumberland Plateau. James White founded the town in 1791, and it was incorporated in 1815. The city covers 104.2 square miles, about 98.5 of them land, and the Tennessee River runs through downtown as part of Fort Loudoun Lake after the Holston and French Broad rivers meet in the southeast.

Ridges give the city its shape. Elevations run from just over 800 feet along the riverfront to more than 1,000 feet on West Knoxville hilltops, with Sharp's Ridge in North Knoxville reaching 1,391 feet. The climate is humid subtropical, with just under 52 inches of precipitation a year and about 36 days at or above 90 degrees. Summers are hot and humid.

The housing stock follows the city's growth. Fourth and Gill, Parkridge and Fort Sanders grew up along the old streetcar lines and hold many Victorian and bungalow houses. Sequoyah Hills and Lindbergh Forest were early automobile suburbs with 1920s and 1930s styles. Bearden and Fountain City joined the city when it annexed them in 1962. Knox County Schools runs the public schools, with 89 schools according to Wikipedia, and the University of Tennessee's flagship campus is a steady source of renters and buyers. TVA, Pilot Flying J and the Discovery media networks have a base in the city, and I-40, I-75, I-640, I-275 and the Pellissippi Parkway (I-140) tie it together.

Census Bureau QuickFacts for Knoxville city:

  • Estimated population on July 1, 2025: 202,021, up 6.0% from the 2020 base
  • Owner-occupied housing rate, 2020 to 2024: 46.6%, so most households rent
  • Typical owner-occupied house, by value: $239,700
  • Median gross rent: $1,191, with 86,263 households
  • Mean commute: 20.2 minutes

How is a Knoxville property tax bill figured?

The assessor appraises the property, applies a percentage set by use, and the taxing bodies multiply that assessed figure by their rates per $100. The assessor's guide lists the percentages: 25 percent for residential and farm property, 40 percent for commercial and industrial, 30 percent for business personal property and 55 percent for public utilities. A house appraised at $100,000 therefore carries an assessed value of $25,000.

Knox County follows a two-year reappraisal cycle, so values are reset more often here than in counties on a longer cycle. In between, the assessor adds new construction and reviews part of the county each year. An Assessment Change Notice has to go out when a value or classification changes. The county commission and city council set the rates, not the assessor, and the city says it does not appraise anything itself.

Current city and county rates are not listed here, since they change with the budget. Ask the Revenue Office for the city rate and the Trustee for the county rate, or read both off the most recent bill for the parcel.

When is Knoxville property tax due, and is the discount still open?

City tax is due October 1 and turns delinquent on March 1 of the following year. The 1 percent city discount ended at the close of October, so on November 15, 2026 it is no longer available for this tax year. Once March 1 passes, the city adds penalty and interest of 1 percent each per month.

The discount applies only to real estate tax, never to personal property or public utility tax. The city also applies each payment to the oldest unpaid year first, so a delinquent balance from a prior year absorbs money meant for the current bill. The Trustee takes county payments in person, online at propertytax.knoxcountytn.gov, by phone at 865-215-2305 option 3, or by mail. Its software vendor charges 2.5% on a credit card and $1.00 on an e-check, and the city's online payment fees likewise go to its vendor and not to the city.

DateWhat happensSource
October 1City tax dueCity of Knoxville, Property Taxes
End of October1% city discount ends (passed for 2026)City of Knoxville, Property Taxes
March 1City tax delinquent, 1% penalty and 1% interest monthlyCity of Knoxville, Property Taxes

How do I appeal a Knoxville assessment?

Begin with an informal talk with the assessor at 865-215-2360, then go to the county's equalization board if that fails. The assessor lists three valid grounds: your value is too high, another owner's value is too low, or the classification is wrong, such as commercial listed as residential. The amount of tax is never a ground, since the rate is not the assessor's decision.

The county board meets beginning June 1. A disputed assessment generally has to go there first or it becomes final. From the county board you can appeal to the State Board of Equalization by August 1 or within 45 days of the date the county board's notice was sent, whichever is later. The state board starts with a hearing before an administrative judge, who issues a decision within 90 days of the hearing. A taxpayer who still disagrees can petition a chancery court within 60 days after the state board's order becomes final. The Comptroller's appeals page walks through each step. This year's June window is closed, so an owner who missed it should wait for the next tax year's notice cycle.

What tax relief can a Knoxville homeowner claim?

The Trustee's relief page lists a state credit and a freeze. The credit pays part of the bill. It is not an exemption, so the full bill still arrives and the owner pays it.

  • Elderly and disabled homeowners: up to $85 for 2026, with combined 2025 income for all owners capped at $38,470.
  • Disabled veterans and their widows or widowers: up to $444, with no income limit, for an owner whose service-connected rating is permanent and total.
  • Senior freeze: owners 65 or older by December 31, 2026 can freeze the base tax on one home and up to five acres, with a 2025 income cap of $63,470 that counts VA income.

Each program needs a yearly application, and the Assessor's site gives April 5 as the apply-by date. The city's Revenue Office at 865-215-2084 also answers relief questions for city tax.

What happens to tax when a Knoxville house sells?

Tax stays with the house, whatever the contract says. The city states that unpaid tax becomes the new owner's obligation even when the seller agreed to pay it, and that private agreements do not change the city's right to collect. A buyer should ask the Revenue Office for the bill on the parcel, and a seller who owes back tax should get the payoff figure early, from both the city and the Trustee.

Prorating is a matter between the buyer and seller, usually handled by the title company at closing. A seller with a balance, a pending appeal or an inherited house to clear can ask the title company how each item will appear on the settlement statement. Tennessee also holds tax sales for delinquent parcels: the Trustee's page shows a June 2, 2026 sale at the Grande Event Center on Clinton Highway, where bidders had to be current on their own taxes. Clearing an old balance before listing keeps a Knoxville house out of that process.

More questions about Knoxville, TN Property Tax Guide

Does the City of Knoxville collect the same tax as Knox County?

No, they are two separate taxes. The city bills its own rate through the Revenue Office and the county bills its rate through the Trustee. A house inside city limits normally receives both bills, and each office has its own phone number and payment address.

Can I still get the Knoxville city discount this year?

No. The 1 percent discount closed at the end of October, and today is November 15, 2026. The full amount is due now, and delinquency begins March 1 of next year.

Who should I call if my Knoxville assessment looks too high?

Call the Knox County Property Assessor at 865-215-2360 for an informal review. That conversation is not an appeal, so to keep your rights, file with the county's equalization board, which sits beginning June 1.

Will a buyer owe my unpaid Knoxville tax?

Yes, the lien follows the property. The city says unpaid tax becomes the new owner's obligation even if the seller promised to pay, so a title company usually collects any balance from your proceeds at closing.

How do I find out whether I qualify for relief on a Knoxville home?

Check the Trustee's relief page or call the Trustee at 865-215-2305. You must own the home and live in it, and income limits apply to the elderly and disabled credit and to the senior freeze. Applications are due by April 5.

  • Tennessee structure: county Assessor of Property values; county Trustee collects county taxes; each city either collects its own levy or uses the county Trustee. Hamilton, Shelby, Knox, Davidson etc. differ as noted.
  • Tennessee: county Assessor of Property values property; county Trustee collects county taxes; cities either collect their own or contract with the county Trustee.
  • Nashville is a consolidated city-county (Metropolitan Government); the Metropolitan Trustee collects the combined real property tax.

Nashville by the numbers

Who sends the property tax bill in Nashville?

Two Metro offices share the job. The Assessor of Property decides what your house is worth for tax purposes, and the Office of the Metropolitan Trustee mails the bill and takes the payment.

Nashville and Davidson County run as one Metropolitan Government, so the Trustee describes its role as the tax collector for the county. Besides real property, the office collects personalty and public utility taxes, runs the state tax relief, tax deferral and tax freeze programs, and handles delinquent taxes, Central Business Improvement District taxes, Gulch district taxes and vegetation liens. The Assessor's office is at 700 President Ronald Reagan Way, Suite 210, Nashville, TN 37210.

  • Tax billing and collection, including payoff questions: 615-862-6330
  • Mortgage inquiries at the Trustee: 615-862-6330
  • Tax relief and tax freeze applications: 615-862-6140
  • Assessor call center for appeal appointments: 615-862-6059

How is a Nashville property tax bill figured?

The Trustee's calculator page lists four pieces: appraised value, assessment ratio, assessed value and tax rate. The assessor sets the appraised value. State law sets the ratio at 25 percent for residential and farm property, 40 percent for commercial and industrial property and 30 percent for personalty.

The Metro Council sets the rate, and it is not final until the State Board of Equalization certifies it. The Trustee page shows two rates, each stated per hundred dollars of assessed value, one for the Urban Services District and one for the General Services District.

Example (Metro Trustee rates)Urban Services DistrictGeneral Services District
Rate per $100 of assessed value$2.814$2.782
Bill on a $100,000 appraisal ($25,000 assessed)$703.50$695.50
Bill on a $417,400 appraisal ($104,350 assessed)$2,936.41$2,903.02

Source: Metropolitan Trustee, Calculate Property Taxes. The $417,400 line uses the Census median owner-occupied value for Davidson County as a stand-in, so your own bill will differ. Your appraisal notice and the Trustee's lookup show the real numbers.

When are Nashville property taxes due?

Statements go out in October, and the Trustee says the tax must be paid in full by the last day of February to avoid interest. For the bill mailed in October 2026, that means February 28, 2027.

You can pay at the Trustee's office or at a First Horizon Bank financial center, which accepts Metro property tax payments from October through February under an arrangement with the Trustee. If a lender escrows your taxes, the servicer normally pays the bill, but the Trustee's mortgage inquiry line can confirm whether a payment posted. Check this before you sign a sale contract, since a missed escrow payment becomes a closing item.

What is the path for contesting a Nashville property value?

You start with the Assessor and, if that fails, go to the independent Metropolitan Board of Equalization. For 2026 both windows have closed: the informal review deadline was April 17, 2026, and scheduling a formal appeal ended at 4:00 p.m. on June 26, 2026. Watch the Assessor's site next spring for the next dates.

The Board of Equalization is created under Metropolitan Charter Article 11, Chapter 2. It has five members appointed by the Mayor and confirmed by the Council, serving two-year terms, and it can send cases to hearing officers. It sits from the first business day of June until that year's equalization is finished. You book through the call center at 615-862-6059.

Bring evidence that supports a lower value as of January 1 of the appeal year:

  • Comparable sales close to your home in age, features and square footage, with size within about 20 percent of yours
  • Any fee appraisal you already hold, understood as an opinion that the board reviews rather than accepts automatically
  • Repair estimates for needed work, not routine upkeep
  • Photographs of damage or outdated kitchens and baths

A relative may file for the owner. Anyone else, including an attorney or tax representative, needs a signed letter of authorization that names the parcel and the assessment year. If the board's decision disappoints you, you have 45 days after the board mails its notice to go to the State Board of Equalization.

What tax relief can Nashville homeowners claim?

Homeowners aged 65 and up, disabled homeowners, disabled veterans and surviving spouses of disabled veterans can apply for state-funded tax relief through the Trustee. The program dates to a 1973 constitutional amendment, and Metro adopted it locally.

The Trustee page for the current window lists an income cap of $38,470 for Davidson County, measured on 2025 income for all owners and a spouse. Applicants must have turned 65 by December 31 of the tax year, show the home is their principal residence, and sign a form that lets the Trustee check income with the IRS, Social Security or the state. Applications run through April 5, 2027, and anyone already enrolled in the relief or freeze programs must return a voucher by April 5 every year to stay in. Call 615-862-6140 before you gather paperwork, because the veteran and spouse routes use separate forms.

What happens when Nashville property tax goes unpaid?

After the last day of February, the bill becomes delinquent and interest applies under Tennessee law. The Trustee's office collects and processes delinquent taxes, so that office is where you ask for a payoff figure that includes interest through a specific closing date.

Liens also matter to a seller. The Trustee collects vegetation liens and the special district taxes mentioned above, so ask whether any of them sit on your parcel. A title company will search for all of them, and an early account history from the Trustee keeps a surprise charge from delaying closing.

How do you sell a Nashville house with tax still owed?

You can sell it. Unpaid property tax is cleared from the sale money at closing, and the title company asks the Trustee for the exact amount.

  • Call 615-862-6330 and ask for the balance, interest and any lien lines on your parcel.
  • Tell the closing agent the date you expect to close so interest is counted to that day.
  • If the house is vacant or inherited, confirm who the Trustee has on file to receive the bill, since a statement mailed to a former owner is easy to miss.
  • Compare any offer with the amount owed, because a low price can leave you short of the tax and loan balances.

Owners facing a large tax balance often weigh a sale to a buyer who closes as-is, which saves repair costs and showing time. Whatever route you choose, get the payoff in writing from the Trustee before you accept terms.

What do the Census numbers say about Davidson County homes?

Davidson County had 745,904 residents in the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate, a 4.2 percent rise over the 2020 base. It lists 389,379 housing units and 324,907 households for 2020 to 2024.

Only 52.8 percent of homes are owner-occupied, so close to half of the county's households rent. The median owner-occupied value is $417,400, owners with a mortgage report median monthly costs of $1,910, and median gross rent is $1,582. Median household income is $77,853. The county issued 5,632 building permits in 2025.

More questions about Nashville, TN Property Tax Guide

Is there a separate Nashville city tax on top of the county tax?

No. Nashville and Davidson County are one government, and the Trustee lists one rate for each service district: $2.814 in the Urban Services District and $2.782 in the General Services District, each per hundred dollars of assessed value. Your tax bill shows which applies to your parcel.

By what date must 2026 Nashville property tax be paid to avoid interest?

The last day of February 2027, which is February 28. The Trustee mails statements in October and says taxes must be paid in full by that date to avoid interest.

Can I still appeal my 2026 Nashville property value?

No new appeal can start for 2026, because the informal review deadline was April 17, 2026 and the formal scheduling deadline was June 26, 2026. If you already had a Metropolitan Board of Equalization hearing, the state board accepts an appeal for 45 days after the notice is mailed.

Who qualifies for Nashville property tax relief?

Owners aged 65 and up, disabled owners, disabled veterans and surviving spouses of disabled veterans, if they meet the income limit. The Trustee lists $38,470 for Davidson County based on 2025 income, and applications are open through April 5, 2027.

Who do I call to find out what I owe before closing?

Call the Metropolitan Trustee's tax billing and collection line at 615-862-6330 and ask for a payoff that includes interest to your expected closing date. Hand the same figure to your title company so the balance comes out of what you receive at closing.

Jackson by the numbers

Which offices handle property tax for a house in Jackson, TN?

Four offices touch a Jackson property tax bill. The Madison County Assessor of Property sets the value, the City of Jackson Revenue Office bills the city tax, and the Madison County Trustee bills the county tax. The county's own tax page says the Assessor takes no payments and mails no bills.

The Revenue Office sits in the west end of City Hall's first floor and keeps weekday hours from half past eight to half past four, closing on national holidays. City tax is paid at the customer service counter. For questions about city payments, call (731) 425-8212. The Trustee, Billy Burkhead, works from Suite 107 at 100 E. Main Street and can be reached at (731) 423-6027, with doors open nine to five. The Assessor, Frances Hunley, is upstairs in Suite 304 at (731) 423-6063, open from half past eight to five.

The Revenue Office also issues city business licenses, so a landlord with a rental in Jackson should ask there whether one applies. The City Recorder keeps ordinances, resolutions and deeds the city holds, and they can be viewed on request.

How does Jackson assess a home, and what rates apply?

The county's estimate calculator lists the assessment percentages below. A Jackson home is taxed on 25% of its appraised value, and the bill is the assessed value times the combined City of Jackson and Madison County rates.

Assessment percentages used by the Madison County Assessor, with a Jackson example
Property classShare of value assessed
Residential25%
Farm25%
Commercial40%
Industrial40%
Personal property (net)30%
Example: house appraised at $217,800 (the Census median for Jackson)$54,450 assessed

The calculator page states that it gives an estimate only and that the 2026 rates for Jackson are the city rate plus the county rate. Tax rates are set each year by the County Commission and the Jackson City Council, so use the calculator or the Revenue Office for the current figures. Neither the Assessor nor the calculator replaces your bill.

When is Madison County's next reappraisal and what has happened to values?

Madison County's next countywide reappraisal is scheduled for 2027, and the last one was in 2022, as required by Tenn. Code Ann. 67-5-1601. Between reappraisals, about one third of parcels are inspected each year for changes to land or buildings.

The Assessor's page reports a median home sale price of $251,450 in January 2026, against $212,500 in January 2022, which it calls an estimated 18.33% increase. Assessment change notices go out by mail, usually in May, only to owners whose value moved up or down. Returned mail is common, so call the Assessor if you moved in the past two or three years.

  • Jackson owners should expect a notice in spring 2027 if their value changes.
  • The county advises owners to contact the Assessor first and confirm the property record is correct before appealing.

What is the appeal path for a Jackson assessment?

Start with a call to the Assessor to check the property record, then appear before the Madison County Board of Equalization. Its five members own property in Madison County or the City of Jackson, and they sit on weekdays through the first two weeks of June. You can book a slot in the last two weeks of May.

Only the current year's value is open to challenge: the county's example is that 2025 taxes cannot be appealed in 2026. A homeowner who loses at the county board can go to the State Board of Equalization. The county page gives the filing limit as August 1 or forty-five days after the date on the county's notice, whichever falls later. The state fee is partly nonrefundable, $10 to $17. Pay the undisputed part of the bill before it goes delinquent while the case is open.

Evidence the Assessor asks homeowners to bring:

  • Sales of similar nearby homes dated in the one or two years before the tax year under appeal.
  • A recent fee-based appraisal.
  • Photos of the exterior and interior condition.

What tax relief can Jackson homeowners apply for?

Elderly homeowners, disabled homeowners, disabled veterans and widows or widowers of disabled veterans can apply through the Madison County Trustee. The Trustee's page asks applicants to bring a driver's license, Medicare card, Social Security card, proof of income for the applicant, spouse and all owners of the property, and a title or bill of sale if the home is a mobile home.

The county also lists a state property tax freeze program. The Tennessee Comptroller notes that relief reimburses taxes after you pay, so you still need to pay each bill, and that relief covers only your primary residence. Call the Trustee at (731) 423-6027 for the current application period.

Online payment through the city covers real property, which is land and buildings, and personal property, which is business equipment. A homeowner will normally have only a real property bill and needs the parcel ID or street address to find it.

What does a seller owe at closing when a Jackson house has tax due?

The title company asks both the City Revenue Office and the Trustee for payoffs, since a home inside Jackson carries a city and a county bill. The Madison County page says homes within city limits should contact the City Revenue Office at (731) 425-8212 and also the County Trustee at (731) 423-6027, while homes outside the city deal with the Trustee alone.

The Assessor updates mailing addresses for both billing offices, so a new owner should ask the Assessor to change the address after the sale. For parcels outside Jackson, check whether the property sits in the City of Three Way or Humboldt, which the county calculator lists with their own rates.

If you do not know your parcel ID, the city's payment guide shows how to look up a property by address through the public records search.

What is Jackson like for a house seller?

Jackson is the Madison County seat, 70 miles east of Memphis and 130 miles southwest of Nashville. It was founded in 1821, named for Andrew Jackson, and became a railroad hub from 1851 onward. The Census Bureau estimates 69,339 residents for 2025, up from 68,205 in 2020, across about 58 square miles of land.

For 2020-2024 the Census Bureau shows 51.2% of Jackson homes occupied by owners, a $217,800 median value for those homes, $1,145 in median gross rent, and $53,032 in median household income. About 22.2% of residents live in poverty, and the city has 27,541 households. The average commute is 18.2 minutes.

Union University, Lane College and Jackson State Community College are in the city, and the Jackson-Madison County School System serves local students. Downtown has a designated Arts District with the Carl Perkins Civic Center nearby.

More questions about Jackson, TN Property Tax Guide

Where do I pay City of Jackson property tax?

Pay at the Revenue Office in City Hall on weekdays, or use the city's online portal for real and personal property. The phone number for city payment questions is (731) 425-8212.

Who collects Madison County property tax?

The Madison County Trustee, Billy Burkhead, collects it at 100 E. Main Street, Suite 107, Jackson. Call (731) 423-6027 to reach the office.

When is the next property reappraisal in Madison County?

The next countywide reappraisal is scheduled for 2027. The previous one took place in 2022. Notices of changed values are mailed by the Assessor, usually in May.

When can I appeal my Jackson assessment?

Use the Madison County Board of Equalization in the first two weeks of June, with appointments opening in late May. Only the current year's assessment can be appealed.

Does the Madison County Assessor send tax bills?

No. The Assessor sets values only and does not accept payments or mail bills. The City Revenue Office bills city tax and the County Trustee bills county tax.

Hendersonville by the numbers

Who sends a property tax bill to a Hendersonville homeowner?

A house inside Hendersonville is taxed twice, by Sumner County and by the City of Hendersonville, and the two bills come from different offices. The Sumner County Trustee collects the county share, and the city's finance office collects the city share. The Sumner County Assessor of Property sets the value both bills use.

Hendersonville is the largest city in Sumner County, on Old Hickory Lake about 18 miles northeast of Nashville. Its city hall is at 101 Maple Drive N, Hendersonville, TN 37075. The Trustee's office is in Gallatin at 355 North Belvedere Drive, Room 107, phone (615) 452-1260, open weekdays from eight to four-thirty. The Assessor can be reached at (615) 452-2412.

What are the Hendersonville and Sumner County tax rates?

The city's Tax Structure page lists a Hendersonville rate of $0.5883 per $100 of assessed value and a Sumner County rate of $1.4210 per $100. Together that is $2.0093 per $100 of assessed value. Residential and farm property is assessed at 25% of appraised value, commercial and industrial at 40%, and personal property equipment at 30%.

Worked example for a $400,000 Hendersonville house, using the city's posted rates
StepAmount
Appraised value$400,000
Assessed value at 25%$100,000
City tax at $0.5883 per $100$588.30
County tax at $1.4210 per $100$1,421.00
Combined annual tax$2,009.30

The Board of Mayor and Aldermen approves the city budget each year in a process of about three months, with two readings and a public hearing before it takes effect. That hearing is where a change in the city rate would surface.

Rates can change when the city and county adopt new budgets, so ask the finance office and the Trustee for the figures on your own bill. Census figures for 2020-2024 show a $430,700 median owner-occupied value in Hendersonville, so the example sits a little below a typical home here.

When is Hendersonville property tax due and how can I pay it?

City taxes can be paid from the first Monday in October and are due by the last day of February. Interest of 1.5% a month starts March 1. The county bill follows the same February deadline, and Sumner County adds interest from March 1 as well.

  • City bill by mail: send a check payable to the City of Hendersonville to 101 Maple Drive N. The postmark date counts as the payment date.
  • City bill in person: City Hall takes cash, check, money order or card, and a dropbox on the front portico is open around the clock for checks and money orders.
  • City bill online: through the city's online payment portal. Cards add a 2.95% convenience fee, and an e-check carries a $2.95 fee.
  • County bill: online at tnpayments.com, by mail with the top of the notice, by phone, at Room 107, or at local banks listed on the back of the notice. Cards cost 2.65% plus $1.

The Trustee takes up to five partial payments by check or cash. Any unpaid portion starts collecting interest on March 1.

How do I challenge a Hendersonville assessment?

Contact the Sumner County Assessor at (615) 452-2412 for an informal review, then use the Sumner County Board of Equalization, then the State Board of Equalization. For tax year 2026 the informal window ran May 4 to May 29 and the county board convened June 1. The last day to book a county board appointment was June 12, so that period is over.

The assessor's site says the next informal reviews should start in May 2027, with formal appeals for tax year 2027 heard from June 1, 2027. Sumner's last countywide reappraisal notices went out in 2024. The assessor lists the kinds of evidence it accepts for homes:

  • Sales of comparable properties.
  • Recent photographs.
  • Insurance replacement value or a recent appraisal.
  • Costs to build, and the cost to cure any physical or functional problem.
  • Changes in the physical characteristics of the property.

Is there tax relief for Hendersonville homeowners?

Sumner County's Trustee runs the state relief program for elderly, disabled and disabled veteran homeowners, and also a tax freeze program for the county and part of the county's cities. Ask the Trustee whether the freeze covers your Hendersonville address, because the county describes it as covering only a portion of the cities.

Relief for people 65 and older and for disabled homeowners is income based. Relief for totally and permanently disabled veterans, and for their surviving spouses, is not. Applications are taken when the tax bills are mailed and must be finished no later than 35 days after the February payment deadline. Freeze applications for 2026 began in September 2026, and annual requalification is required. To book a phone or online appointment, call (615) 452-1260.

The Tennessee Comptroller adds that relief is a payment toward the tax, not an exemption, so you still receive and must pay your bills. Relief applies to a primary residence only.

What happens to property tax when a Hendersonville house sells?

Both the city and the county bill stay with the parcel, so the closing agent should pull a payoff from each office. Sumner County shows verification of paid taxes under the online payment link, which helps confirm that a prior year is clear.

The Assessor's office handles mailing address changes for county bills, so call (615) 452-2412 after closing so notices reach the new owner. Questions about tax sales in Sumner County go to the Clerk and Master's office.

Deeds are recorded with the Sumner County Register of Deeds, which publishes its own records site. Under state rules the grantee, meaning the buyer, pays the transfer tax.

What should a Hendersonville seller know about the city?

Hendersonville had 61,753 residents in the 2020 census and about 64,266 in the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate, the tenth largest city in Tennessee. The city has 25,255 households, and owners occupy 71.7% of homes. Rent runs a median $1,653, household income a median $97,200, and the mean commute is 29.7 minutes.

State Route 386 and U.S. 31E carry most traffic. A tornado struck the city on December 9, 2023, so ask for permit records on any house that had storm repairs. The city is governed by a mayor and twelve aldermen. Sumner County Schools serve Hendersonville, including Hendersonville High, Beech High, Ellis Middle and Merrol Hyde Magnet School.

Indian Lake Village, along Indian Lake Boulevard, is one of the city's main shopping and dining districts and mixes retail, offices, medical space and homes.

Hendersonville has roughly 47.9 inches of rain a year at the Old Hickory Dam station, with hot summers, so gutters and drainage are worth checking before you list.

More questions about Hendersonville, TN Property Tax Guide

Does Hendersonville have its own property tax?

Yes. The city levies $0.5883 per $100 of assessed value on top of the Sumner County rate of $1.4210. The city collects its own bill at 101 Maple Drive N, and the county Trustee collects the county bill in Gallatin.

When are Hendersonville property taxes due?

They are due by the last day of February. Payments open on the first Monday in October, and interest of 1.5% per month starts March 1. Mailed payments count on the postmark date.

How can I pay Hendersonville property tax online?

Use the online payment portal linked from the city's Tax Structure page. Cards carry a 2.95% convenience fee and e-checks a $2.95 processing fee, and both fees may change.

Can I still appeal my 2026 Hendersonville assessment?

No. The Sumner County Board of Equalization finished its 2026 session, and the last appointment day was June 12. Informal reviews for tax year 2027 are expected to start in May 2027.

Who do I call about senior tax relief in Hendersonville?

Call the Sumner County Trustee at (615) 452-1260. Applications are accepted when bills are mailed and until 35 days after the February deadline, and the office books appointments by phone or online.

Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $458,300 here, which is 64% above the middle figure for the 28 Tennessee places. About 19% of households rent, so 81% own; the Tennessee median for these places is 61% owner-occupied. Homes here were typically built in 1997, so the median house is about 26 years old. These numbers describe Collierville as a whole, so a given street can sit well above or below them.

Who bills what in Columbia

  • Maury County Assessor of Property handles assessment.
  • City of Columbia bills and collects the tax.

Due dates

City of Columbia page: real and personal property taxes are due and payable without penalty from November 1 through December 15. County taxes follow the state calendar (first Monday in October through February; Maury Trustee search excerpt).. See the official page.

Challenging your assessment

Tennessee process: optional informal review with the county Assessor of Property (not an appeal), then formal appeal to the county board of equalization (meets June 1; Shelby County convenes May 1), then the State Board of Equalization by August 1 or within 45 days of the county board notice, whichever is later (TN Comptroller). Failure to appeal to the county board generally forfeits further appeal rights.. See the official page.

Tax rate

The official page we opened lists Columbia: Maury County rate 1.91000 + city rate 0.82510 = total 2.73510. Per $100 of assessed value; TN Comptroller county summary page (page last modified 24 Sep 2024, tax year not shown) - may not equal the current-year adopted rate.. See the official page.

Columbia by the numbers
